key_terms.meaning: Fixing the relative positions of points on or near the earth and drawing them to scale on a map or plan
Surveying that treats the earth's surface as flat; used when the survey area is small enough that curvature error can be ignored
Surveying that accounts for the earth's curvature and uses a reference ellipsoid; used for large areas
Survey of land parcel boundaries for ownership records and land registration
Survey that fixes both horizontal position and elevation of natural and man-made features
How close a measured value is to the true value
How closely repeated measurements of the same quantity agree with each other
An error that follows a physical law or instrument defect, has the same sign and size under the same conditions, and can be corrected by a formula
Ratio of map distance to the corresponding ground distance, written as 1:S
A defined reference surface plus origin and orientation against which coordinates are computed
The equipotential surface of the earth's gravity field that best fits mean sea level, extended under the land
A mathematically smooth surface of revolution that approximates the geoid and is used for coordinate computation
Height of a point above the geoid, measured along the plumb line; the height shown by levelling
A permanently marked point of known reduced level to which all levelling in an area is referred
Distance of a point measured along the base line from the start point, usually in metres
A short measurement taken at right angles (or at a known angle) from a survey line to a detail point
Fixing intermediate points on a straight survey line between two end stations
Electronic distance measurement: distance found from the travel time or phase change of an electromagnetic wave sent to a target
Accuracy written as ±(a + b ppm × D), where a is a constant in mm, b is the scale error in parts per million and D is the measured distance in km
A small fixed correction added for the path inside the prism and the offset between instrument and prism vertical axes

takeaways: Surveying has one job: fix relative positions of points and draw them to scale, working from the whole to the part.
Plane surveying ignores curvature, geodetic surveying does not; the choice depends on the area and the accuracy needed.
Accuracy is closeness to truth, precision is repeatability; a set of readings can be precise and still wrong.
Gross errors are mistakes and are removed by re-measurement; systematic errors are corrected by formula; random errors are reduced by averaging.
Scale 1:S means one unit on the map equals S units on the ground, so a 1:1000 map is more detailed than a 1:25000 sheet.
Every coordinate needs a datum: an ellipsoid, a geoid, an origin and an orientation; heights above the geoid are orthometric heights and h = H + N.
Tape survey builds a skeleton of base, tie and check lines with offsets; tape corrections make the reading a true horizontal distance.
EDM replaces the chain; its accuracy is quoted as a fixed part plus a part proportional to distance, and atmospheric and prism corrections must be applied.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to state the principle of surveying, separate plane from geodetic, list and correct tape/EDM errors with formulas, and explain datum and coordinate concepts with a sketch.

bank.q: State the two basic principles of surveying and explain why surveying proceeds from the whole to the part.
outline: First principle: work from the whole to the part, fix a control framework of high accuracy first, then fill in detail.
Second principle: fix a point by at least two independent measurements (two distances, two angles, or distance and bearing).
Prevents accumulation of errors, keeps detail consistent with control, allows checks at every stage.
Example: control traverse first, then offsets from it.

bank.q: Classify surveys by purpose, by instrument used and by the treatment of the earth's curvature, giving one use for each type.
outline: By purpose: topographic, cadastral, engineering, control, hydrographic, astronomical.
By instrument: chain/tape, compass, theodolite, total station, GNSS.
By curvature: plane surveying (small areas, flat earth) versus geodetic surveying (large areas, ellipsoid).
One practical use for each class, stated in one line.

bank.q: Distinguish between accuracy and precision, and between gross, systematic and random errors, with one example of each.
outline: Definitions of accuracy and precision; the four combinations of high/low.
Gross error: observer mistake, wrong booking, wrong reading; detected by repeats.
Systematic error: tape too long, temperature, refraction; same sign and magnitude, corrected by formula.
Random error: pointing and reading, small and both signs, reduced by averaging, follows a error curve.

bank.q: Explain what a datum is. Describe the geoid, the reference ellipsoid and the relation between ellipsoidal height, orthometric height and geoid undulation.
outline: Datum = reference surface + origin + orientation + (for modern datums) an ellipsoid.
Geoid: mean sea level surface extended under land; ellipsoid: mathematical approximation.
h = H + N, define each symbol and its units.
Why a coordinate without a datum is meaningless; mention WGS84 as a geocentric datum.

bank.q: Define scale. Distinguish a large-scale map from a small-scale map, and list the marginal information found on a topographic sheet.
outline: Scale = map distance / ground distance = 1:S.
1:1000 is large scale, 1:50000 is small scale; large scale shows more detail over a smaller area.
Marginal information: sheet number and name, scale, contour interval, north direction, legend, benchmark values, adjoining sheet index.
Plain statement of the representative fraction and graphic scale.

bank.q: A 30 m steel tape is standard at 20 degrees C and 100 N tension, with cross-sectional area 3 square mm and weight 0.25 N per metre. Explain each correction needed when it is used to measure a sloping line in the field, and write the formula for each.
outline: Standardisation: Ca = (L' - L)/L times measured length, L' and L in m.
Temperature: Ct = L times alpha times (Tm - Ts), alpha = 11.2e-6 per degree C for steel.
Tension (pull): Cp = (P - Po) L / (A E), E about 2e5 N per square mm.
Sag: Cs = -(w squared l cubed)/(24 P squared), negative, so measured > true.
Slope: Ch = L(1 - cos theta), or Ch = square root of (L squared - h squared) with h the level difference.
Alignment: correction for ends off the line.
State the sign of each correction.

bank.q: An EDM gives an accuracy of plus or minus (3 mm + 3 ppm). Compute the expected error for distances of 100 m, 1 km and 5 km and comment on which term dominates.
outline: Formula: error = a + b times D in km.
Constant term dominates at short range, ppm term at long range.
State that atmospheric correction and prism constant must also be applied.

bank.q: Describe the field procedure for a chain and tape survey of a small plot: ranging, base line, tie lines, check lines and offsets, and how the plot is drawn afterwards.
outline: Reconnaissance and sketch of the area, fix stations so lines are unobstructed.
Direct ranging by eye and by line ranger between stations; indirect ranging when ends are not intervisible.
Measure base line and all tie and check lines; book in a field book with a neat diagram.
Take perpendicular and oblique offsets with a cross staff or optical square, note chainage and offset in metres.
Check: the check line computed from the plotted triangle must agree with the measured value.
Plot to scale, fit offsets, compare with the check line, correct closing error if any.

bank.q: A tape 30 m long is found to be 0.02 m too short. It measures a line as 1200 m at a temperature of 35 degrees C when standardised at 20 degrees C. Apply the standardisation and temperature corrections and state the true distance.
outline: Standardisation: correction per tape = -0.02 m, so correction = (0.02/30) times 1200 with the sign that a short tape over-reads.
Ct = 1200 times 11.2e-6 times (35 - 20).
Combine the two corrections with signs.
State final true distance in metres to two decimals and note that sag and slope are not given, so not applied.

bank.q: Compare chain and tape surveying with EDM and total station work for a topographic survey of a 5 hectare site. Judge which you would choose and justify.
outline: Chain and tape: cheap, no power, accurate for short distances, slow, limited by ground and obstructions, errors accumulate with many offsets.
EDM and total station: measures slope distance and angles, reduces to coordinates in the field, longer range, needs calibration and atmospheric correction.
Compare initial cost, speed, accuracy per point, manpower, data handling.
Justify a choice with the site size, terrain and required accuracy; note that a control framework is needed either way.
Mention GNSS as the control option.

bank.q: A student claims that averaging many readings removes all error. Evaluate this claim using the ideas of gross, systematic and random errors.
outline: Averaging reduces only random errors, roughly by 1 over square root of n.
Systematic errors survive averaging; they shift the mean and need a formula or calibration.
Gross errors distort the mean badly; they must be found and removed first.
Conclusion: accuracy needs correction plus averaging, not averaging alone.
Give a tape example: a tape 0.05 m too long stays wrong however many times it is used.

bank.q: Explain why a latitude and longitude pair without a stated datum, and a height without a stated reference surface, are of limited use in engineering work.
outline: Same physical point gets different coordinates on different datums; shifts can be tens to hundreds of metres.
Datum transformation converts coordinates between datums; parameters must be stated.
Height may be ellipsoidal (GNSS) or orthometric (levelling); they differ by the geoid undulation N.
Engineering uses: setting out, GIS overlay, flood levels; a wrong datum gives a wrong position or level.
Recommend recording datum, epoch and projection with every coordinate set.

bank.q: Assess the sources of error in an EDM observation and suggest practical steps to keep a total station traverse within 1 in 10000 closing accuracy.
outline: Instrument errors: zero error, scale error, prism constant, phase resolution.
Atmospheric errors: temperature and pressure affect wave speed; enter corrected values or let the instrument do it.
Pointing and centring errors, prism alignment, height of instrument and target.
Reflectorless measurement: weaker return, shorter range, larger error, careful on dark or inclined surfaces.
Practise: forced centring, measure each distance both ways, close the traverse, adjust by Bowditch or transit rule, apply curvature and refraction to long lines.

glossary.def: The art and science of determining the relative positions of points on or near the earth's surface and representing them to a convenient scale on a map or plan.
Surveying in which the curvature of the earth is taken into account and computations are made on a reference ellipsoid.
A survey that establishes a network of points of known high accuracy to which all detail surveys are referred.
Surveying of water bodies to fix depths, shore lines and underwater features for navigation and dredging.
Surveying in which positions are fixed from observations of stars, giving latitude, longitude and azimuth independent of ground control.
The difference between a measured value and the true value of the quantity.
A small error of unpredictable sign and size, caused by imperfect observation, which is reduced by repeated measurement and averaging.
The difference between an observed value and its adjusted or most probable value.
A scaled, conventional representation of features of the ground seen from above on a horizontal plane.
The scale written as a ratio 1:S, where one unit on the map equals S of the same units on the ground.
The constant vertical distance between two successive contour lines on a map.
Latitude, longitude and height that define a position on a stated reference surface.
Plane coordinates, such as easting and northing in UTM, obtained by mathematically projecting the ellipsoid onto a flat surface.
The set of parameters and formulas used to convert coordinates from one geodetic datum to another.
The average height of the sea surface over a long period, used as the zero for heights.
The height of the geoid above (or below) the reference ellipsoid at a place, symbol N, in metres.
The longest and most carefully measured line of a chain survey, from which the framework of the survey is built.
A line measured in the field only to verify that the plotted framework is correct.
An offset measured at 90 degrees to the survey line, usually with a cross staff or optical square.
The ruled notebook in which all field measurements and sketches are recorded at the time of survey.
An instrument that measures distance by transmitting an electromagnetic signal to a reflector or target and measuring phase or time of travel.
The frequency at which the carrier wave of an EDM is varied; it sets the unit of length used to resolve the phase difference.
A correction applied to EDM distances for the actual temperature and pressure, since the speed of light in air depends on both.
